books.section: Topic 6.12 Controversies over the Role of Government in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: J. F. Jarvis, 'Coxey's Army approaching Washington,' stereograph, 1894

stimulus.text: Stereograph photograph, “More Money! Less Misery! Good Roads!” Coxey’s Army approaching Washington, copyright 1894 by J. F. Jarvis. A column of unemployed men marches along a dirt road toward Washington, led by a man on horseback. Banners in the march read “More Money! Less Misery! Good Roads!” and “Death to Interest on Bonds.” The marchers set out from Massillon, Ohio, on March 25, 1894, and reached Washington on May 1 with about 500 men.
stimulus.source_note: J. F. Jarvis stereograph, copyright 1894, sold by Underwood & Underwood; Library of Congress, LC-DIG-stereo-1s09209. Public domain: photograph published 1894 (pre-1930). Banner wording checked against the image; march dates and numbers follow the standard account of Coxey's Army.

stem: Why did Coxey’s marchers carry a banner reading “Death to Interest on Bonds”?

options.text: They wanted the government to borrow more money at high interest
options.misconception: The banner calls for the death of interest, not for more borrowing at interest.

options.text: They wanted banks to charge farmers higher interest rates
options.misconception: The marchers wanted relief from debt, not higher rates for farmers.

options.text: They wanted the government to print paper money for roads
They wanted to abolish all money and return to barter
options.misconception: The banners call for 'More Money,' not for an end to money.

rationales.A: 'Death to Interest' rejects borrowing at interest, so more borrowing is the opposite.
rationales.B: The marchers wanted relief from debt, not higher interest rates.
rationales.C: Background from the books: Coxey's bill would print $500 million in Treasury notes for roads.
rationales.D: The banners call for 'More Money,' not for an end to money.
rationales.general:
Ask what the banner is against.
1. 'Death to Interest on Bonds' attacks paying interest to bondholders.
2. Background from the books: Coxey's Good Roads bill would print $500 million in Treasury notes.
3. Paper money for roads would put men to work without borrowing at interest.
4. The banner is a demand for printed money, not for more borrowing or no money.
Remember: a protest slogan names the enemy, so ask who pays and who gains.
